title: Abel-Ruffini Galois Theory Extensions
description: Extends the Abel-Ruffini formalization with the complete solvability classification of symmetric groups. Proves S₀–S₄ are solvable, S_n is solvable if and only if n ≤ 4, A₅ is simple (the key obstruction), and non-commutativity witnesses for S₃, S₄, S₅, A₄, A₅. Verifies group orders |S₇|=5040, |S₈|=40320, |A₇|=2520, |A₈|=20160 via `native_decide`. 59 theorems (57 public + 2 private), 15 typeclass instances (11 public + 4 private), 1 private definition (`klein_four`), 0 sorries. The `native_decide` group-order and non-commutativity certificates depend on the `Lean.ofReduceBool` axiom (axiomCount = 1).

overview.historicalContext:
The quest for formulas solving polynomial equations spans millennia. The quadratic formula was known to Babylonian mathematicians (~2000 BCE). The cubic formula was found by Scipione del Ferro (~1515) and published by Cardano (1545); the quartic by Ferrari (1540), also in Cardano's Ars Magna. In 1799, Ruffini gave an incomplete argument that the quintic has no radical solution; Abel (1824) gave the first rigorous proof of quintic unsolvability. Galois (1832), in a letter written the night before his fatal duel, laid down the complete theory: a polynomial equation is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable. The key group-theoretic fact is that $S_n$ is solvable for $n \leq 4$ (via composition series with abelian factors) but not for $n \geq 5$ — because $A_5$ is simple and non-abelian, appearing as an insoluble composition factor. The simplicity of $A_5$ (the unique normal subgroups of $A_5$ are $\{e\}$ and $A_5$ itself) was proved by Galois. The threshold $n = 4$ is the precise boundary, explaining the existence of Cardano's cubic and Ferrari's quartic formulas while blocking any general quintic formula. Two intermediate steps are essential context: **Lagrange (1770)**, in *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations*, introduced the *resolvent* — a function of the roots that becomes the key object permuted by the Galois group — and observed that for $n = 5$ the natural resolvent fails to lower the degree, foreshadowing the eventual obstruction. **Ruffini (1799)**, in *Teoria generale delle equazioni*, gave the first detailed argument that no general radical solution exists in degree five; his argument was *largely correct but had a gap*: he tacitly assumed that any radical expressing a root must itself be a rational function of the roots (later proved by Abel's 1826 lemma on natural irrationalities). **Cauchy (1815)** developed the modern theory of permutations and the symmetric group $S_n$, supplying the combinatorial vocabulary Galois would later weaponize. Galois himself coined the term *groupe* in his 1830–1832 manuscripts and was the first to recognize that the *normal* subgroups — and hence the composition series — carry the solvability signal. The Jordan–Hölder theorem (Jordan 1869, Hölder 1889) later proved the composition factors $A_5$ that appear in $S_n$ for $n \geq 5$ are an *invariant* of the group, sealing the obstruction as intrinsic rather than presentation-dependent.

**Extended context (companion gallery entries).** The solvability classification connects to a wide methodological lineage, each strand cross-linked below: Hermite's 1858 elliptic-modular escape and the Tschirnhaus-Bring-Jerrard normal forms as the positive complement (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`); Arnold's 1963 topological proof of the obstruction without Galois theory; the Picard-Vessiot differential-Galois analogue (`abel-ruffini-oq-09`); Cardano's casus irreducibilis on real-radical strictness; the $S_6$ outer automorphism (Hölder 1895) and Schreier's conjecture on $\mathrm{Out}(A_n)$; Frobenius's 1896 character-theoretic proof of $A_5$ simplicity; Hilbert's 1892 irreducibility theorem bridging generic-Galois-group to concrete realizations; Belyi's theorem and Grothendieck's dessins d'enfants; and Stauduhar's 1973 resolvent method underlying the LMFDB. Previously inlined as standalone key-insight essays, these are kept here in digest form and developed in full in the linked entries.
overview.problemStatement: Prove the complete solvability classification: $S_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$ (and $A_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$). Prove $A_5$ is the minimal obstruction (simple and non-abelian). Verify specific group properties and orders. Formalize the Galois connection: non-solvable Galois group implies non-solvability by radicals.
overview.proofStrategy: Fifteen sections organized around major themes. Part I proves small symmetric and alternating groups solvable: $S_0, S_1$ by `isSolvable_of_subsingleton`; $S_2$ by `isSolvable_of_comm` after `decide`; $S_3$ via the short exact sequence $1 \to A_3 \to S_3 \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$ using `solvable_of_ker_le_range`; $S_4$ similarly after proving $A_4$ solvable via the Klein four-group $V_4$ (defined by $x^2 = e$, proved normal by `native_decide`). Part II packages these into the complete biconditional using `interval_cases` and Mathlib's `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`. Parts III-XV add supporting theorems: A₅ simplicity and order, Galois contrapositive, subgroup/quotient/isomorphism solvability, cardinalities (from $|S_2|=2$ to $|S_8|=40320$), non-commutativity witnesses, and factorial identities.
keyInsights: The solvability threshold $n = 4$ has a direct geometric meaning: degree-4 polynomial equations can be solved by repeatedly extracting square and cube roots (Cardano/Ferrari formulas), but degree-5 cannot. This corresponds precisely to the group-theoretic fact that $S_4$ is solvable (has a chain $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ with abelian factors) while $S_5$ is not.

A₅ is the smallest non-abelian simple group: it has no non-trivial normal subgroups and is not commutative. Its order $|A_5| = 60$ makes it significantly smaller than the next example ($PSL(2,7)$ of order 168). Galois's discovery of $A_5$'s simplicity in 1832 was the key insight connecting group theory to polynomial equations.

The proof of $S_4$ solvability requires the Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e, (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23)\}$: a normal subgroup of $A_4$ isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$. This is the deepest case — $A_4$ (order 12) is the smallest group for which the converse of Lagrange's theorem fails: despite $6 \mid 12 = |A_4|$, no subgroup of $A_4$ has order 6. $V_4 = \{x \in A_4 : x^2 = e\}$ is the unique proper non-trivial normal subgroup of $A_4$, making it the only possible intermediate in the composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$.

The Lean proof of the biconditional $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ is remarkably concise: the forward direction uses `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` (5 lines) and the backward direction delegates to Mathlib's `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`. The heavy mathematical work is done inside Mathlib, demonstrating the power of building on a mature library.

**The `solvable_of_ker_le_range` splicing lemma — the central technique behind every $S_n$-solvability proof in this file ($n \leq 4$), and the Mathlib-form of Schreier's 1929 extension theorem.** Mathlib formulates the short-exact-sequence solvability splicing not as the textbook "$H \trianglelefteq G$ with $H$ and $G/H$ both solvable implies $G$ solvable" but as the slightly more general *Schreier extension form*: given a group homomorphism $\phi : G …

A₅'s simplicity has a striking geometric face: $A_5 \cong \text{PSL}(2,5) \cong I$, where $I$ is the group of 60 orientation-preserving symmetries of the regular icosahedron. Felix Klein (1884) showed that solving the quintic reduces entirely to icosahedral geometry — the impossibility of solving quintics by radicals is equivalent to the impossibility of decomposing the icosahedron's symmetry group into an abelian composition series.

**Derived length and radical depth**: The derived (commutator) series of $S_4$ is $S_4 \supset A_4 = [S_4,S_4] \supset V_4 = [A_4,A_4] \supset \{e\} = [V_4,V_4]$, giving $S_4$ a derived length of 3 — it takes exactly 3 commutator steps to reach the trivial group.

**Sylow counting forces $A_5$ simplicity**: This file invokes `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` from Mathlib as a black box, but the underlying counting argument is itself remarkable. From $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, the Sylow theorems force the Sylow numbers to be $n_2 \in \{1, 3, 5, 15\}$ with $n_2 \equiv 1 \pmod 2$, $n_3 \in \{1, 4, 10\}$ with $n_3 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, and $n_5 \in \{1, 6\}$ with $n_5 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$.

**Lagrange resolvents — the pre-Galois precursor**: 60 years before Galois, Lagrange (1771, *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations*) gave a uniform recipe explaining *why* Cardano's cubic and Ferrari's quartic formulas existed: for an $n$-th degree equation with roots $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ and a primitive $n$-th root of unity $\zeta_n$, the **Lagrange resolvent** $L_\sigma = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \zeta_n^k \alpha_{\sigma^k(1)}$ for …

**Discriminant square test detects $A_n$ vs $S_n$**: The qualitative classification proved here ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$) has a concrete computational counterpart — the **discriminant square test**. For an irreducible $f \in F[x]$ of degree $n$ with roots $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ in a splitting field, the **discriminant** $\Delta(f) = \prod_{i < j} (\alpha_i - \alpha_j)^2$ lies in $F$ (it is a symmetric function of the roots).

**The generic Galois group is $S_n$ — why this group-theoretic classification governs *equations* (van der Waerden's theorem)**: The result proved here ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$) bears on Abel-Ruffini only because $S_n$ is the Galois group of the *general* degree-$n$ polynomial — a fact this file uses implicitly but never states.

conclusion.summary: Proves the complete group-theoretic backbone of Abel-Ruffini: $S_n$ is solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ and $A_n$ is solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ — the precise reason why polynomial equations of degree $\leq 4$ are solvable by radicals but degree 5 is not. The key obstruction is $A_5$: the smallest non-abelian simple group ($|A_5| = 60$), whose simplicity forces any composition series of $S_5$ to include $A_5$ as an insoluble factor, blocking the abelian-factor chain that solvability requires. The 59 theorems across 15 sections — including non-commutativity witnesses, group order computations, sign-kernel identity, and Galois connection formalization — form a self-contained ($0$ sorries; the `native_decide` group-order and non-commutativity certificates depend on `Lean.ofReduceBool`) reference implementation of the complete solvability classification in Lean 4 using Mathlib. The accompanying keyInsights compendium situates the result in five distinct mathematical traditions that all converge on the same $A_5$-obstruction: (i) the *geometric* face via the icosahedral group $I \cong A_5 \cong \mathrm{PSL}(2,5)$ and the McKay/$E_8$ correspondence (insights #6, #2); (ii) the *topological* face via Arnold's 1963 monodromy proof using $B_5$, derived series, and the discriminant complement (insight #12); (iii) the *transcendental* face via Hermite's 1858 modular-form solution of the quintic in $\theta$-constants over $\Gamma(5)$ and Klein's icosahedral form (insight #11); (iv) the *combinatorial-character-theoretic* face via Cauchy class-size arithmetic, Sylow counting, Frobenius character tables, and Brauer modular representations (insights #8, #19, plus the cycle-type interpretation in the Part XV annotation); and (v) the *algorithmic/verification* face via the discriminant square test, Stauduhar's resolvent method, the LMFDB Galois-group database, and Lean's `decide`/`native_decide` boundary (insights #10, #16, #24). Together these reveal that the $n = 4$ solvability threshold proved here is not a single theorem but a *boundary* in a five-dimensional intellectual landscape where algebra, geometry, topology, arithmetic, and computation each independently detect the same simple non-abelian $A_5$ as the minimal obstruction.
conclusion.implications:
1. **Closure of a 300-year quest**: The biconditional $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ definitively explains why Cardano's cubic and Ferrari's quartic formulas exist but no analogous quintic formula can exist — the Galois groups $S_3, S_4$ have composition series with abelian factors, while $S_5$ does not because $A_5$ is simple and non-abelian.

2. **Entry point to the classification of finite simple groups**: $A_5$ (order 60) is the smallest non-abelian simple group and the first entry in the monumental Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG, completed 2004, ~10,000 pages). The solvability boundary at $n = 4$ is precisely where the first non-abelian simple composition factor appears: the composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_5 \trianglelefteq S_5$ has the non-abelian simple factor $A_5/\{e\} \cong A_5$, while $S_5/A_5 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian — the obstruction is $A_5$ itself as a composition factor, not the top quotient.

3. **Differential Galois theory (Picard-Vessiot)**: The identical solvability obstruction governs linear ODEs with rational coefficients. A homogeneous linear ODE $L(y) = 0$ is solvable by quadrature (iterated integration, exponential, algebraic operations) if and only if its differential Galois group — a linear algebraic group — is solvable. This Picard-Vessiot theory is the ODE analogue of classical Galois theory.

mainTheorems.name: symmetric_solvable_iff
mainTheorems.description: Complete classification: the symmetric group $S_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$. The forward direction discharges five cases by `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` (delegating to the small-$n$ instances built in Part I); the reverse direction packages `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` via `by_contra; push_neg; omega`. This is the file's principal contribution to the gallery — the qualitative classification that, paired with Galois's solvability theorem (Mathlib `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`), yields Abel-Ruffini for the generic quintic.

mainTheorems.name: alternating_solvable_iff
mainTheorems.description: The alternating-group analogue: $A_n$ is solvable if and only if $n \leq 4$. The reverse direction follows by subgroup heredity from `symmetric_solvable_iff` ($A_n \leq S_n$); the forward direction goes through the sign-kernel exact sequence — were $A_n$ solvable for $n \geq 5$, then `solvable_of_ker_le_range` applied to the sign exact sequence would make $S_n$ solvable, contradicting the symmetric threshold. Combined with `symmetric_solvable_iff`, this pins the solvability boundary at $n = 4$ from both sides.

mainTheorems.name: a5_simple
mainTheorems.description: $A_5$ is a simple group (no non-trivial normal subgroups). The central obstruction underlying every non-solvability result in the file: $A_5$ simple and non-abelian forces it to appear as a non-cyclic composition factor in $S_n$ for all $n \geq 5$, blocking any abelian-factored composition series. Delegates to Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`, which internally runs the Sylow-counting argument detailed in keyInsight #8 ($n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$, all $\neq 1$).

mainTheorems.name: not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois
mainTheorems.description: Contrapositive of Galois's solvability theorem: if the Galois group of a polynomial is not solvable, then no root is expressible by radicals. Composes Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` (forward direction of Galois's theorem) with negation via `intro hsol; exact hns (... hsol)` — a three-line proof bridging this file's group-theoretic classification (`symmetric_solvable_iff`, `a5_simple`) to the analytic statement of Abel-Ruffini. The named theorem makes the contrapositive directly citable in downstream proofs without unfolding the implication.

mainTheorems.name: sign_kernel_is_alternating
mainTheorems.description: The keystone identity $\ker(\mathrm{sgn} : S_n \to \{\pm 1\}) = A_n$ as a formal equality between subgroups. Proved by `ext` + `Equiv.Perm.mem_alternatingGroup`, this two-line theorem translates the abstract kernel of the sign homomorphism into the concrete alternating subtype and is the linchpin on which every short-exact-sequence argument in Part I pivots — used three times to lift solvability across $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$ (for $n = 3, 4$) and $1 \to V_4 \to A_4 \to A_4/V_4 \to 1$.

mainTheorems.name: galois_group_order
mainTheorems.description: The order of a finite Galois group equals the extension degree: $|\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)| = [E : F]$. Direct invocation of Mathlib's `IsGalois.card_aut_eq_finrank` under the standard hypotheses `[FiniteDimensional F E] [IsGalois F E]`. Establishes the numerical shadow of the Galois correspondence — the bijection between intermediate fields and subgroups in cardinality form — and provides the file's interface to extension degrees from downstream proofs that need to read off $|\mathrm{Gal}|$ from $[E:F]$.

mainTheorems.name: solvable_small_has_abelian_factors
mainTheorems.description: Joint solvability packaging for $n \leq 4$: simultaneously certifies $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(S_n)$ AND $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(A_n)$ as a single anonymous-constructor proof $\langle \text{symmetric\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn,\ \text{alternating\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn\rangle$. While `symmetric_solvable_iff` and `alternating_solvable_iff` give the full biconditional classifications, this paired conjunction is the form most directly consumed by downstream proofs that need *both* solvability witnesses to construct composition series with abelian factors (the canonical $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$ tower for $n \leq 4$, refined by $V_4$ at $n = 4$). Flagged as an original contribution in `meta.originalContributions[3]`: bundles two Mathlib instance inferences into a single ergonomic API surface without requiring re-derivation at the call site.
